start_here.title: New here? Do this first
steps: Pick one app: ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini. The free version is fine to start, and you can always switch.
Check your privacy setting. It takes two minutes. See "Your data" in level 0.4.
Do the level 0.0 try-its, then pick one build from Start building. Make something today.

ten_hours: Wharton professor Ethan Mollick's rule of thumb: AI starts to click after about ten hours of real use. Use it on stuff you already know, so you can tell when it's wrong.

jagged-frontier.title: Jagged frontier
jagged-frontier.definition: AI is amazing at some things and weirdly bad at others, and the split isn't what you'd guess. The only way to find the edges is to try it on your own stuff.
jagged-frontier.think: A genius who still can't fold a fitted sheet.

your-data.title: Your data
your-data.definition: On free and personal plans, your chats can be used to train future models unless you switch that off in settings. Either way, don't paste in passwords, account numbers or anything you'd hate to see again.
your-data.think: Talking in a coffee shop. Mostly fine, but you lower your voice for some things.

bias.title: Bias
bias.definition: AI learned from human writing, so it picked up our blind spots too, like picturing every CEO as a man. Notice it, and ask for other angles.
bias.think: A mirror that can also magnify.

human-in-the-loop.title: Human in the loop
human-in-the-loop.definition: You stay the one who checks and signs off, especially before AI sends, buys or posts anything for you. Your name is on it, not the AI's.

levels.name: Say hi
levels.promise: You don't need to know how it works to start. You need a few words and one good habit.
try: Ask for a birthday message twice. First just "write a birthday message." Then write it like a text to a smart friend: who it's for, how you know them, one inside joke, how long. Compare the two.
Ask it for a fact with a source. Click the source. Does it exist and say what the AI claimed?
Snap a photo of your fridge and ask what you can make for dinner.
check: In one sentence, what's the difference between a model and an app?
Why does a better prompt usually beat a better model?
Name one time you'd double check an AI answer before using it.

levels.name: Make it yours
levels.promise: Stop re-explaining yourself every chat. Set it up once and it starts smarter every time.
try: Write three lines of custom instructions: who you are, how you like answers, and one thing to never do.
Start a project for one ongoing thing in your life, like a trip, a job search or a class. Add one file.
Give the same planning question to the regular mode and to the thinking mode. Which answer would you actually use?
check: What's the difference between memory and custom instructions?
When is a small, fast model the right pick?
What kind of question is worth a deep research report?

levels.name: Spot the traps
levels.promise: AI fails quietly and confidently. These are the ways it happens, and the easy habits that protect you.
try: Open Settings and find the privacy or data controls. Decide on purpose whether your chats can be used for training.
Share an idea you like and ask: "What would a smart skeptic say? Be blunt." Compare that to its first reaction.
Pick a family safe word you'd ask for if "you" ever called asking for money.
check: What's one thing you'd never paste into a chatbot?
What are two signs a piece of writing is AI slop?
Why is prompt injection a bigger deal once AI can take actions for you?

levels.name: Under the hood
levels.promise: Just enough of how it works to follow the news, ask good questions and not get fooled by hype.
try: Search "tokenizer" and paste in a sentence. Watch how it gets chopped into tokens.
Upload a long PDF and ask three questions, each with the page number of the answer. Check one.
In a very long chat, ask what you said in your first message. Did it slip?
check: Why do long chats sometimes get worse?
RAG or fine-tuning: which one would you use to answer questions about your company handbook, and why?
Why do AI companies care so much about GPUs and data centers?

levels.name: AI that does things
levels.promise: The jump from answering questions to actually getting stuff done for you, with you still in charge.
try: Vibe code something tiny, like the dinner bill splitter in Start building. Use it once for real.
Connect one app you already use, like your calendar or Drive, and ask it to find something for you.
Give an agent a job with a clear finish line, like "find three Saturday hikes under an hour away and put them in a table."
check: What makes something an agent and not just a chatbot?
What's one task you'd hand to an agent, and one you wouldn't yet?
What would you want to approve before AI clicks buy or send for you?

levels.name: The big questions
levels.promise: The debates everyone is having. Nobody has the answers yet, so your take counts.
try: Pick one big question below. Write your own opinion in three sentences before you ask AI anything.
Then ask AI for the strongest argument against you. Did it change your mind or sharpen it?
Bring it up at dinner. See where people land.
check: If AGI arrived tomorrow, how would you know?
Who should decide what AI is allowed to do?
What's one thing you'd never hand to AI, no matter how good it gets?

builds.title: What's for dinner?
builds.why: The fastest way to see what multimodal means
builds.prompt: Here's a photo of my fridge. Give me three dinners I can make tonight with what's in here, plus anything I'd need to grab. Keep each one under 30 minutes.

builds.title: Teach it your voice
builds.why: Every draft after this sounds a little more like you.
builds.prompt: Interview me one question at a time about how I write: who I usually write to, words I use a lot, and things I'd never say. After eight questions, write a short voice guide I can paste into my custom instructions.

builds.title: Quiz me, don't tell me
builds.why: Use AI to learn faster without letting it do the thinking.
builds.prompt: I'm learning [topic]. Quiz me one question at a time. Don't give me the answer until I've tried. If I'm wrong, give me a hint first, then the answer.

builds.title: Your own coach
builds.why: A project that remembers your goal and checks in on it
builds.prompt: You're my coach for [goal]. Start by asking me five questions about where I am now and what gets in my way. Then give me a plan for this week. Every time I come back, ask how it went before you give advice. Be honest, not a cheerleader.

builds.title: Build a tiny app
builds.why: You just made software. No code required.
builds.prompt: Make me a simple, colorful web app that splits a dinner bill. I type the total, the tip and everyone's names, and it shows what each person owes. Make it easy to use on my phone.

builds.title: Plan the party
builds.why: We planned parts of our wedding this way. It handles the boring logistics so you can do the fun part.
builds.prompt: I'm planning [event] for [number] people on [date] with a budget of [amount]. Ask me what matters most first. Then give me a timeline, a checklist and three ideas that would make it feel like us.

builds.title: Settle a debate
builds.why: Our favorite use. It won't pick a side, and that's the point.
builds.prompt: My partner and I disagree about [topic]. Give the strongest case for each side, then tell us what evidence would change each of our minds. Don't pick a winner.

builds.title: Clear your week
builds.why: Figure out what AI should do for you, and what you should still do yourself.
builds.prompt: Here's everything on my plate this week: [paste your list]. Sort it into three piles: things AI could do for me, things AI could help me do, and things I should do myself. Explain each pick in one line.

stuck: Show it, don't describe it. Paste an example you love and say "more like this."
Tell it exactly what's off, like you'd tell a new coworker. Then ask it to double check its own answer.
Ask "What would a smart skeptic say?" or "What am I missing?"
Long chats slip. Start a fresh chat with a quick summary, or keep the work in a project.
You don't know what to ask.
Let it interview you: "Here's my week. What could you help with?"

model-vs-app.definition: OpenAI is the company. GPT is its family of models. ChatGPT is the app you open. Same idea for Anthropic, Claude models and the Claude app.

model-sizes.definition: Most AI companies sell a few sizes of the same model. Bigger is smarter, smaller is faster and cheaper, and the names change every few months.

gpu.definition: The chips that do AI's heavy math. Nvidia makes most of them, and every AI company wants more.

first_week: Do the three level 0.0 try-its. Birthday message twice, fact check, fridge photo
Write your three lines of custom instructions and start one project
Two minutes in privacy settings. Then ask for a smart skeptic's take on an idea you love
Pick something you're learning and run the Quiz me, don't tell me prompt
Make the dinner bill splitter, then use it at dinner
Run the debate prompt on something you and a friend actually disagree about
Sort next week into three piles: AI does it, AI helps, you do it
